leads.EN: Astronauts used this entry to board Discovery and exit after landing. Today, it still serves as the primary access point for Museum staff. Click "Read More" for a video tour of the interior.

imageAltText.EN: A man looks out of the window of the space shuttle while it is in orbit. The view out the windows looks blue, perhaps from Earth's oceans.
A man looks out of the window of the space shuttle while it is in orbit. The view out the windows looks blue, perhaps from Earth's oceans.
A space shuttle orbiter against the black background of space, as seen from above. The payload bay door is open.

leads.EN: These gray panels are made of heat-resistant reinforced carbon-carbon. They shielded areas subject to the hottest temperatures during reentry, up to 3000°F (1650°C)—the nose cap and wing leading edges
Black tiles protected areas that reached from 1200°F to 2300°F (650 to 1260°C) on the underside and were coated with black glass.
White tiles protected areas around the forward windows and OMS pods that reached less than 1200°F (650°C). White tiles do not have glass coating like the black tiles do.
Blankets protect the orbiter's sides because they were lighter, easier to install, and required little maintenance. Made of flexible woven silica strands, their texture is quilted and smooth.
NASA chose delta (triangular) wings over straight wings for greater maneuverability.
Like an airplane, Discovery also features retractable landing gear for a smooth landing on a runway. They are stowed during launch and reentry for a more thermally stable and aerodynamic surface.

imageAltText.EN: A very small chamber with drawers in the walls and at the center a toilet.

leads.EN: The drag chute door would open upon landing to release a parachute to help slow the vehicle down as it rolls down the runway.

imageAltText.EN: A space shuttle orbiter touches back down on earth. Its drag chute has been deployed from the aft of the vehicle.

leads.EN: The body flap serves two purposes. It acts like an airplane’s horizontal stabilizer, keeping the vehicle’s attitude level. It’s also large to protect the main engines during atmospheric reentry.
Also known as the tail, the vertical stabilizer kept the orbiter lined up with its direction of motion. Two large panels, or speed brake, could be flared out, to slow the vehicle after touchdown.
Found on either wing, elevons are like the ailerons that control roll on aircraft. For Space Shuttle orbiters, which do not have elevators, the elevons also control pitch.
What you are looking at is the Space Shuttle Discovery. Discovery is an example of a Space Shuttle orbiter, a component of NASA’s Space Transportation System (STS).
Join space shuttle curator Jennifer Levasseur on a tour through the interior of Discovery.

leads.EN: The orbiter’s main engines worked together with two solid rocket boosters (not seen here) to provide the orbiter with enough thrust to launch into space.
Once in orbit, the standard forces of flight on we use to fly aircraft on Earth no longer apply.

leads.EN: Discovery features windows that aid in the variety of missions it carried out while in service.
Discovery features a payload bay the size of a school bus.

leads.EN: Just like on Earth, astronauts needed a place to use the bathroom while in space.

leads.EN: The shuttle was designed for maximum reusability. It needed to be able to safely glide onto a runway when it touched back down to Earth.
